papers.title: Pro-China YouTubers in digital diplomacy: Effects of source nationality and profession on credibility, trust, media engagement, and attitudes toward China
papers.authors: Qiuyue Cho-Li, Rebecca Frazer, Tse-hsi Chien, and Spiro Kiousis
papers.category: 甲亢哥访华 · direct foreign-audience mechanism
papers.evidence: Publisher or authoritative index record verified
papers.takeaway: A 2 × 2 between-subjects online experiment with census-matched U.S. adults manipulated presenter nationality (American versus Chinese) and profession (vlogger versus journalist) in pro-China public-diplomacy content. Chinese presenters were judged more credible than American presenters, perceived similarity mediated the nationality effect on credibility, and credibility positively predicted trust in Chinese state media, media-engagement intentions, and attitudes toward China. This is the closest direct evidence for the IShowSpeed idea because it tests foreign audiences, influencer-like sources, engagement intentions, and attitudes toward China, although it does not examine a real-time visit or IShowSpeed followers.

papers.title: Reimagining Belonging on rednote: Cross-Cultural Social Media Migration and Media Dependency
papers.category: X automatic translation · adjacent platform-translation evidence
papers.evidence: Publisher or authoritative index record verified
papers.takeaway: Semi-structured interviews with 29 American RedNote users examine how people adapted after migrating to a culturally unfamiliar platform. Participants reorganized media goals, negotiated language and cultural barriers, and described platform usability, translation support, and informal guidance from other users as resources that made early participation manageable and supported continued involvement and belonging. This is adjacent platform evidence rather than a direct X study: translation is embedded in a broader adaptation process, and the qualitative design does not isolate causal effects on replies, reposts, interaction depth, or relationship formation.

papers.title: Perceived artificial intelligence job displacement as an occupational health concern: when meaningful work intensifies workaholism and burnout
papers.authors: Wei Xu, Yong Liu, Wenxian Wang, Hyeran Choi, and Seung-Wan Kang
papers.category: Workplace AI and well-being · direct evidence
papers.evidence: Publisher or authoritative index record verified
papers.takeaway: A two-wave, one-month time-lagged survey followed 337 employees in China's information and communication technology industry. Perceived AI job displacement, job meaningfulness, and workaholism were measured at Time 1 and burnout at Time 2. Perceived displacement was positively associated with burnout and workaholism, workaholism carried an indirect association with burnout, and job meaningfulness strengthened the displacement-to-workaholism path and the resulting indirect effect. The temporal separation improves measurement ordering but the nonexperimental self-report design does not establish causal effects.

papers.title: Daily job crafting with generative artificial intelligence: Implications for work meaningfulness and engagement
papers.authors: Neris Güven, Almasa Sarabi, and colleagues
papers.category: Workplace AI and well-being · direct daily-diary evidence
papers.evidence: Publisher or authoritative index record verified
papers.takeaway: A ten-workday diary study followed 149 full-time employees in the United Kingdom who used generative AI at work. Four forms of GenAI-driven job crafting—augmenting instrumental resources, augmenting social resources, augmenting challenging demands, and automating hindering demands—showed different daily relationships with engagement through autonomy, competence, relatedness, and subsequent work meaningfulness. The competence pathway received the most consistent support, whereas the relatedness pathway was weakest. The repeated-measures design captures within-person daily variation but remains observational.

papers.title: AI, Human, and Organizational Factors Associated with Work Loneliness
papers.authors: Constance Hadley and Sarah L. Wright
papers.category: Preprint · workplace AI and well-being · not peer reviewed
papers.evidence: Publisher or authoritative index record verified
papers.takeaway: A cross-sectional survey of 1,545 U.S. employees who used AI at least monthly examines workplace loneliness alongside AI use, social confidence, perceived leader caring after AI introduction, and organization-sponsored social opportunities. Relative-importance analyses attribute substantially more explanatory weight to human and organizational conditions than to AI variables, suggesting that loneliness in AI-enabled work is not reducible to technology exposure alone. The design is correlational, and this SSRN working paper has not completed journal peer review.

toc.title: Recommending the state: How social media algorithms curate state-created content in China
toc.abstractEn: An analysis of 119,064 trending and recommended Bilibili videos combines descriptive statistics, regression models, and Markov-chain simulation to assess algorithmic amplification of state-created content. State-produced videos, especially news and politics, were disproportionately recommended, and state accounts occupied self-reinforcing recommendation pathways. The evidence concerns observed platform outputs rather than direct access to the ranking code.

toc.title: Through their eyes: neural and behavioral evidence for enhanced immersion via point-of-view editing
toc.abstractEn: Thirty-nine adults watched eight original narrative films in point-of-view and matched control edits while researchers collected functional neuroimaging, eye-tracking, and behavioral data. Point-of-view editing increased attention to faces and recognition performance, consistent with enhanced immersion through shared attention and inferred intentionality. The controlled film stimuli support mechanism testing but may not generalize to longer or naturally selected viewing.

toc.title: Modes of dialogic communication, modes of reality
toc.abstractEn: This theoretical article contrasts dualistic and nondualistic modes of dialogue using process-relational philosophy and Dzogchen. It develops 'awaring' as a mode of communication and organizes the account around ground, expression, and fruit. The contribution is conceptual rather than an empirical test.

toc.title: Media emotion regulation and executive functions: individual differences in temporal ordering among young children
toc.abstractEn: Six waves of Project M.E.D.I.A. data spanning ages 2.5 to 7.5 are used to model heterogeneity in the ordering of media-based emotion regulation and executive function. Most children followed a bidirectional pattern, while smaller groups showed media-emotion-regulation-driven or diverging trajectories; parent depression also differentiated class membership. The longitudinal design strengthens temporal analysis but remains based on observational developmental data.

toc.title: ‘Communicating in the Air Force’: the National Society for the Study of Communication, the Journal of Communication, and U.S. military education, 1950–1962
toc.abstractEn: Archival research and close textual analysis reconstruct the relationship among the National Society for the Study of Communication, the Journal of Communication, and Air University. The article argues that this partnership shaped military curricula and reinforced a vocational, efficiency-oriented, command-and-transmission conception of communication during the field's institutional formation.

papers.title: Promises and pitfalls of community moderation on social media
papers.authors: Isabelle Augenstein, Michiel A. Bakker, Tanmoy Chakraborty, David P. Corney, and colleagues
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 123(48), e2518033123
papers.category: 综合顶刊 · social media governance
papers.evidence: Publisher or authoritative index record verified
papers.takeaway: This interdisciplinary review and stakeholder analysis evaluates the shift by platforms such as X and Meta toward crowd-sourced fact-checking systems including Community Notes. It synthesizes evidence on scalability, trust, participation, source use, and vulnerability to uneven contributor participation or coordinated manipulation, and it identifies conditions under which community moderation can complement rather than replace professional evidence and platform accountability. The article is a current social-science synthesis rather than a new causal experiment.

papers.title: The Evolution of the Visual Symbols of the Chinese Mythological Character Nezha from the 12th to the 21st Century
papers.venue: Wacana Seni Journal of Arts Discourse, 25(2)
papers.evidence: Publisher or authoritative index record verified
papers.takeaway: This diachronic study traces changes in Nezha's visual symbols from the twelfth through the twenty-first century. It combines image typology, semiotic analysis, and cross-media comparison to examine how a mythological figure moves from ritual and moral meanings toward individualized expression and interactive popular-culture functions. The article does not test foreign audiences, value congruence, identification, or sharing intentions, so it is retained only as adjacent evidence about the construction of the character stimulus that overseas audiences may later receive.

papers.title: Regional Reception of Early Chinese Mythology and Chinese Cultural Identity
papers.venue: Frontiers of Literary Studies in China, 20(1), 1–36
papers.evidence: Publisher or authoritative index record verified
papers.takeaway: This historical and theoretical article examines how early Chinese myths were received, localized, and reorganized across regions and how those processes contributed to the formation of Chinese cultural identity. It treats reception as selective adaptation rather than passive transmission and therefore helps specify how a myth can be reinterpreted across cultural boundaries. It does not study contemporary foreign audiences or experimentally separate comprehension, liking, character identification, and transmission intention, so its relevance is conceptual and adjacent.
